question: If you strip a complete ring of bark from around a tree's trunk but leave the wood underneath untouched, the tree will usually die within a year or two, even though it keeps drawing up water and leafing out at first. Why?
correct_answer: Bark carries sugars down; roots starve
alternative_answers: The phloem in the bark is cut, so food can't reach the roots
Sugars from the leaves can no longer travel down to the roots
The roots starve because nutrient flow in the bark is severed
Girdling cuts the tree's food-transport layer
The roots die from lack of food and then the tree can't take up water
headline_answer: Bark carries sugars down; roots starve
source_excerpt: Girdling results in the removal of the phloem, and death occurs from the inability of the leaves to transport sugars (primarily sucrose) to the roots.

extra.verification_notes: Girdling removes phloem, so sugars can't reach the roots and they starve, while the xylem keeps carrying water; this matches the claimed answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Girdling).

explanation: A tree moves things in two separate systems. Water and minerals travel upward through the wood, the xylem, so an intact trunk still delivers water to the leaves. But the sugars the leaves produce travel downward through the phloem, a thin living layer in the inner bark. Removing a full ring of bark severs the phloem completely, so no sugar can reach the roots. The roots slowly starve, stop growing and eventually stop taking up water, and the tree dies. This is called girdling or ring-barking, and foresters and farmers have used it deliberately for centuries to kill unwanted trees.

question: Wine corks are punched from the thick outer bark of which kind of tree?
source_excerpt: It is the phellem layer of bark tissue which is harvested for commercial use primarily from Quercus suber (the cork oak)

extra.why_interesting: Most people never connect the stopper in a wine bottle to a living tree that is peeled, not felled, and goes on growing new bark for a century.
extra.verification_notes: Cork is harvested mainly from the bark of the cork oak (Quercus suber), and stoppers are its main use, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cork_(material).

explanation: The cork oak is stripped by hand about every nine years and simply regrows its bark, which is why Portugal's cork forests are centuries old and still productive.

question: True or false: green tea and black tea are harvested from two different species of plant.
source_excerpt: Green tea: unwilted and unoxidized. Black tea: wilted, sometimes crushed, and fully oxidized.

extra.why_interesting: The colours and flavours differ so much that many assume separate plants, but the entire difference happens after harvest.
extra.verification_notes: Both green and black tea are made from Camellia sinensis, differing only in processing/oxidation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tea).

explanation: Both come from the very same shrub, Camellia sinensis. Black tea leaves are simply allowed to oxidise and darken after picking, while green tea leaves are heated quickly to stop that process.

question: Bamboo can grow taller than a house and is used for scaffolding, yet botanically it is a giant member of which plant family?
source_excerpt: Bamboos are a diverse group of mostly evergreen perennial flowering plants making up the subfamily Bambusoideae of the grass family Poaceae.

extra.why_interesting: Something that forms forests and is used as scaffolding feels like a tree, yet it is a cousin of the lawn.
extra.verification_notes: Bamboo is the subfamily Bambusoideae of the grass family Poaceae, and it is used for scaffolding, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bamboo.

explanation: Bamboo is a woody grass, and it grows like one: some species shoot up nearly a metre in a single day, making them the fastest-growing plants on Earth.

question: The Venus flytrap looks like it belongs in a tropical jungle, but in the wild it grows naturally only in a small patch of coastal wetland in which country?
source_excerpt: native only to the coastal bogs of North and South Carolina in the United States, specifically within a 100-kilometer (62-mile) radius of Wilmington, North Carolina.

extra.why_interesting: Carnivorous plants read as exotic jungle creatures, but this one is a homebody from the American southeast.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Venus flytrap is native only to coastal bogs of North and South Carolina, USA; Florida and Washington populations are introduced.

explanation: Its entire native range lies within about 100 kilometres of Wilmington, North Carolina. Every flytrap anywhere else in the world descends from that one corner of the Carolinas.

question: The tumbleweed rolling through countless Hollywood Westerns is not native to America at all. From which country was it accidentally imported in the 1870s, hidden in a shipment of flaxseed?
source_excerpt: flaxseed from Russia turned out to be contaminated with Salsola seeds

extra.why_interesting: The single most American image in cinema is an immigrant that arrived by accident after the Wild West era had already begun.
extra.verification_notes: Standard accounts say tumbleweed arrived in South Dakota in the 1870s in flaxseed from Russia; a minor Ukraine variant exists, but the region was then in the Russian Empire.

explanation: It is known as Russian thistle, and it arrived in South Dakota around 1873 in contaminated flaxseed. Within two decades it had rolled across most of the western United States.

question: The same hydrangea bush can bloom pink in one garden and blue in another. Which property of the soil decides the colour?
source_excerpt: An acidic soil (pH below 7) will usually produce a flower colour closer to blue, whereas an alkaline soil (pH above 7) will produce flowers of a pink, or even a red colour.

extra.why_interesting: Gardeners assume colour is bred into the plant, but the same bush can change colour if you move it or change what you feed it.
extra.verification_notes: Soil pH (acidity) controls hydrangea colour via aluminium availability: acidic gives blue, alkaline gives pink, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Acidic soil frees up aluminium that the plant absorbs, turning the blooms blue, while alkaline soil keeps them pink. Gardeners add aluminium sulfate or lime to steer the colour.

question: Three of these vegetables are close relatives in the same plant family as deadly nightshade and tobacco. Which one is not?
source_excerpt: The family Solanaceae contains such important food species as the potato (Solanum tuberosum), the tomato (Solanum lycopersicum), the pepper (Capsicum sp) and the aubergine or eggplant (Solanum melongena).

extra.why_interesting: Three everyday vegetables are close cousins of a famous poison plant, and the intuitive outlier (tomato, a 'fruit') is actually a member.
extra.verification_notes: Potato, tomato and aubergine are Solanaceae along with deadly nightshade and tobacco; cucumber is Cucurbitaceae (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solanaceae).

explanation: Potato, tomato and aubergine are all nightshades, which is why Europeans once feared tomatoes were poisonous. The cucumber belongs to the gourd family, alongside melons and pumpkins.

question: In the wild, which common fruit is really an inside-out bundle of hundreds of tiny flowers, pollinated by a wasp that crawls in through a hole at its tip?
source_excerpt: A small opening or ostiole, at the apex of the fruit, is a narrow passage that allows the specialized fig wasp, Blastophaga psenes, to enter and pollinate the flowers.

extra.why_interesting: You never see a fig tree in bloom because the flowers are inside the fruit, and the pollinator has to crawl into it.
extra.verification_notes: Fig is a syconium (inverted cluster of many tiny flowers) pollinated by a fig wasp entering via the ostiole at the apex; no newer development contradicts this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ficus_carica).

explanation: That is why you never see a fig tree flowering: the blossoms bloom hidden inside. Each wild fig species has its own tiny wasp partner, a relationship tens of millions of years old.

question: In 2005 a seed excavated at the ancient fortress of Masada, about 2,000 years old, was planted and sprouted into a tree nicknamed Methuselah. What kind of tree is it?
source_excerpt: In March 2005, one of the ancient date seeds germinated, becoming the oldest seed in the world successfully sprouted. Dr. Sallon named the seedling 'Methuselah'.

extra.why_interesting: A seed older than Christianity, dug out of a ruined desert fortress, simply woke up and grew.
extra.verification_notes: Methuselah is a date palm grown from a ~2,000-year-old Masada seed that germinated in 2005 (seed dug up in the 1960s, planted 2005); no newer event contradicts this.

explanation: It is a Judean date palm, a variety praised by Roman writers that had vanished for centuries. Methuselah turned out to be male, so researchers later sprouted ancient female seeds to produce fruit.

question: Pando in Utah looks like a forest of about 47,000 trees, but it is one organism sharing a single root system across 43 hectares. Which tree is it?
source_excerpt: Pando... quaking aspen (Populus tremuloides)... approximately 47,000 stems... 42.89 hectares

extra.why_interesting: What looks like an ordinary forest is one individual, heavier than a dozen blue whales, and possibly thousands of years old.
extra.verification_notes: Pando is a quaking aspen clone of about 47,000 stems over 42.89 ha, per Wikipedia; no newer developments change this.

explanation: Every trunk of this quaking aspen is a genetically identical shoot from one root network, estimated to weigh around 6,000 tonnes. The colony is thought to be thousands of years old, though it is now struggling against grazing deer.

question: Six trees of one species growing within two kilometres of the Hiroshima bomb's hypocentre survived the blast of 1945 and are still alive today. Which tree, a familiar sight on city streets worldwide, is it?
source_excerpt: Six ginkgo trees located 1–2 km from the Hiroshima bomb site survived the blast

extra.why_interesting: The species is already the sole survivor of a 200-million-year-old lineage, and then it survived an atomic bomb too.
extra.verification_notes: Ginkgo is the species cited for six survivors near the Hiroshima hypocentre; the per-species count could not be fully confirmed on the Hibakujumoku page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hibakujumoku).

explanation: The ginkgo is the last survivor of a lineage with fossils over 200 million years old, and its toughness showed again at Hiroshima, where the scorched trees budded the following spring. Seeds from them are now planted around the world as peace trees.

question: Young sunflowers famously swing their heads to follow the sun across the sky, but once the flower head matures it stops moving and settles facing one fixed compass direction for the rest of its life. Which direction?
source_excerpt: Circadian regulation of directional growth pathways accounts for both phenomena and leads to increased vegetative biomass and enhanced pollinator visits to flowers.

extra.why_interesting: Almost everyone 'knows' sunflowers follow the sun, so the player expects the answer to be 'they keep turning' or 'south'. The twist is that the grown-up flower parks itself permanently toward the sunrise, and the reason is a charming piece of bee-marketing.
extra.verification_notes: Atamian et al. 2016 (Science) and follow-up drone studies confirm mature sunflower heads stop moving and face east.

explanation: Facing the sunrise lets the head warm up quickly each morning, and researchers found those warm, east-facing flowers attract far more pollinating bees than ones turned the other way.

question: The European Central Bank sets interest rates for the whole eurozone. In which city, not an EU political capital, is it headquartered?
source_excerpt: Seated in Frankfurt, Germany, the bank formerly occupied the Eurotower prior to the construction of its new seat.

extra.why_interesting: Many assume the EU's money is run from Brussels alongside its other institutions; the central bank sits in a German banking city instead.
extra.verification_notes: The ECB is headquartered in Frankfurt, Germany, which is not a political capital, and no relocation is planned (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Central_Bank).

explanation: The bank has sat in Frankfurt since its creation in 1998, the same city that was already home to Germany's Bundesbank and stock exchange.

question: The national currencies of Sweden, Norway, Denmark and the Czech Republic all share a name. What royal object does that name mean?
source_excerpt: Government not to set euro adoption date for now

extra.why_interesting: Players know each currency's name separately but rarely notice four countries across Europe literally spend crowns.
extra.verification_notes: Swedish krona, Norwegian/Danish krone and Czech koruna all mean 'crown', and the Czech Republic has not adopted the euro (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Republic_and_the_euro).

explanation: Each is a local form of the word crown, a legacy of 19th century coins stamped with the monarch's crown, and Czechoslovakia simply kept the name after leaving Austria-Hungary.

question: In September 2008, the largest bankruptcy in American history turned a housing downturn into a global financial crisis. Which 158-year-old investment bank collapsed?
source_excerpt: Lehman's bankruptcy filing is the largest in US history, having beaten the previous record holder Worldcom, Inc.

extra.why_interesting: Most adults lived through the 2008 crash and remember the shock; naming the specific bank that was allowed to fail is the satisfying recall.
extra.verification_notes: Lehman Brothers, founded 1850, filed Chapter 11 on 15 Sept 2008, still described as the largest US bankruptcy (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehman_Brothers).

explanation: Lehman held around 600 billion dollars in assets when it failed, and its collapse froze lending between banks around the world within days.

question: The word dollar comes from a 16th century silver coin named after the mining valley where it was struck. In which modern European country is that valley?
source_excerpt: The Joachimsthaler was minted in Joachimsthal (today Jáchymov) in the Kingdom of Bohemia, now part of the Czech Republic; Thal means 'valley'.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the dollar is an American invention; its name comes from a silver-mining valley in Bohemia.
extra.verification_notes: Joachimsthaler was minted in Joachimsthal (Jáchymov), Bohemia, now the Czech Republic, and is the origin of 'dollar' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachimsthaler).

explanation: The coin was the Joachimsthaler from Joachimsthal, today's Jáchymov in Bohemia, shortened to thaler and eventually Anglicised to dollar.

question: Which medieval military order of monks ran an early international bank, letting pilgrims deposit money in Europe and withdraw it in Jerusalem using a letter of credit?
source_excerpt: deposit their valuables with a local Templar preceptory before embarking, received a document indicating the value of their deposit, then showed that document upon arrival in the Holy Land

extra.why_interesting: Players picture these knights as crusading warriors, not as the medieval equivalent of a travel bank issuing letters of credit.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Templars let pilgrims deposit valuables in Europe and claim equal value in the Holy Land against a document, an early form of banking; no newer event affects this.

explanation: The Templars' network of fortified houses made them bankers to pilgrims and kings alike, and that wealth is part of why the French king crushed them in 1307.

question: Britain's 50 pence coin was the world's first circulating coin with its unusual number of curved sides. How many sides does it have?
source_excerpt: It was the first seven-sided coin in the world.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the coin is not round but rarely count the sides; the curved edges let it roll in vending machines like a circle.
extra.verification_notes: The 50p is a seven-sided Reuleaux-type heptagon and was the world's first seven-sided coin, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Introduced in 1969, its seven curved edges keep a constant width, so it rolls through vending machines as smoothly as a round coin.

question: During Zimbabwe's hyperinflation in 2009, the central bank printed its highest-ever banknote with a face value of one hundred... what?
source_excerpt: the 100 trillion Zimbabwean dollar banknote (10^14 dollars)

extra.why_interesting: Players know Zimbabwe printed huge notes but typically underestimate how far the zeros ran; a single note carried fourteen zeros.
extra.verification_notes: The 100 trillion dollar note (10^14) was issued on 29 January 2009 as the highest denomination, matching 'Trillion'.

explanation: The 100 trillion dollar note carried fourteen zeros and was worth only a few US dollars when issued, and today it sells to collectors for far more than it ever bought.

question: True or false: the economics prize awarded each year in Stockholm was created by Alfred Nobel's will alongside the prizes for physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace.
source_excerpt: not one of the original five Nobel Prizes endowed by Alfred Nobel in his will

extra.why_interesting: Everyone calls it the Nobel Prize in Economics, so players assume Alfred Nobel founded it; it was actually added decades later by a bank.
extra.verification_notes: The economics prize was established by Sveriges Riksbank in 1968, not by Nobel's will, so 'False' is correct (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences).

explanation: Nobel's 1895 will named only five prizes; the economics award was set up in 1968 by Sweden's central bank for its 300th birthday and is officially a prize in his memory.

question: In 2021, which small Central American country, which already used the US dollar as its currency, became the first in the world to make Bitcoin legal tender?
source_excerpt: the first country in the world to use bitcoin as legal tender.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect a crypto pioneer to be a tech hub or a tax haven; it was a small Central American country that already used the US dollar.
extra.verification_notes: El Salvador was the first country to make Bitcoin legal tender (Sept 2021); the 2025 IMF-driven rollback doesn't change the historical past-tense claim.

explanation: President Nayib Bukele's law took effect in September 2021 and the government bought bitcoin for the treasury, though the mandatory acceptance was later softened under pressure from the IMF.

question: Weimar Germany and Zimbabwe are the famous cases, but the worst hyperinflation ever recorded hit a European country in 1946, with prices doubling about every 15 hours. Which country?
source_excerpt: suffering the highest rate of hyperinflation ever recorded in human history... at one stage it took about 15 hours for prices to double

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Germany in 1923 or Zimbabwe, but the all-time record belongs to a European country just after the Second World War.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia says the Hungarian pengő hyperinflation of 1946 was the highest ever recorded, with prices doubling in about 15 hours; I found no newer event that overtakes it.

explanation: Hungary's pengő collapsed so completely that notes for 100 million billion were printed, and in August 1946 it was replaced by the forint, which the country still uses today.

question: The Bank of England dates from 1694, but it is not the world's oldest central bank. Which country's central bank, founded in 1668, holds that title?
source_excerpt: the world's oldest surviving central bank, and the third oldest bank in continuous operation

extra.why_interesting: Players assume England or Italy pioneered central banking; a Scandinavian country beat the Bank of England by a quarter of a century.
extra.verification_notes: Sveriges Riksbank was founded in 1668 and is described as the world's oldest surviving central bank; no contradicting sources or newer developments found.

explanation: Sweden's Riksbank grew out of Stockholms Banco, which had also printed Europe's first banknotes in 1661, and it still sets Swedish interest rates today.

question: In stock-market slang, a long run of rising share prices is named after which animal?
source_excerpt: traders who bought shares on credit were called 'bulls.'

extra.why_interesting: Players have heard the phrase a thousand times but rarely stop to ask why an animal stands for optimism; the folk explanation (a bull tosses its horns upward, a bear swipes its paws downward) is the small 'of course' payoff.
extra.verification_notes: A sustained run of rising prices is a 'bull market', per Wikipedia's Market trend article; no newer developments could change this.

explanation: A bull supposedly attacks by thrusting its horns upward, while its opposite, the bear, swipes downward, so a falling market is a bear market.

question: In 1945, Raytheon engineer Percy Spencer was testing radar magnetrons when a candy bar in his pocket melted. Which kitchen appliance grew out of that mishap?
source_excerpt: a candy bar he had in his pocket melted

extra.why_interesting: A weapon-grade radar component ending up as the most common kitchen gadget is a delightful leap.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Spencer's melted candy bar led to the microwave oven; the patent was filed in 1945, consistent with the question.

explanation: Spencer went on to pop corn and explode an egg with the magnetron, and Raytheon sold the first Radarange ovens two years later.

question: In which year did Alexander Fleming notice that a stray mould had wiped out the bacteria on a neglected culture plate, discovering penicillin?
source_excerpt: On 3 September 1928 he observed by chance that fungal contamination of a bacterial culture (Staphylococcus aureus) appeared to kill the bacteria.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the mould story but often place it during the Second World War, when penicillin was mass-produced, rather than a decade earlier.
extra.verification_notes: Fleming observed the mould killing Staphylococcus on 3 September 1928, per Wikipedia's Penicillin article.

explanation: Fleming spotted the clear ring around the mould in September 1928, but penicillin was not mass-produced until the Second World War, more than a decade later.

question: Charles Goodyear's process of heating rubber with sulfur, which stopped it melting in summer and cracking in winter, takes its name from the Roman god of fire. What is the process called?
source_excerpt: The term vulcanization was suggested by William Brockedon, derived from Vulcan, the Roman god associated with heat and sulfur found in volcanoes.

extra.why_interesting: The player has to connect a mythology clue to a rubber term they have heard on tyre adverts, a satisfying two-step.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the process is named vulcanization after the Roman god Vulcan, and credits Goodyear with the sulfur-heating discovery; Hancock's earlier British patent does not affect the question as worded.

explanation: Goodyear hit on it in 1839 after accidentally dropping a rubber and sulfur mixture on a hot stove, and named it after Vulcan.

question: True or false: the non-stick coating Teflon was invented by NASA scientists during the space program.
source_excerpt: Roy J. Plunkett accidentally discovered PTFE in 1938 while employed at DuPont's facility.

extra.why_interesting: Teflon is one of the most repeated 'NASA spin-offs' in popular belief, yet it predates NASA by twenty years.
extra.verification_notes: Teflon (PTFE) was discovered accidentally by DuPont chemist Roy Plunkett in 1938, twenty years before NASA was founded, so 'False' is correct.

explanation: False. DuPont chemist Roy Plunkett found it by accident in 1938, when a cylinder of refrigerant gas turned into a slippery white powder, two decades before NASA existed.

question: The first ever Nobel Prize in Physics, in 1901, went to a German physicist who in 1895 noticed a screen glowing across his darkened lab while experimenting with cathode-ray tubes. Who was he?
source_excerpt: the first recipient of the Nobel Prize in Physics

extra.why_interesting: Players know X-rays but rarely realise they were the very first physics discovery honoured by a Nobel.
extra.verification_notes: Röntgen was the first Physics Nobel laureate (1901) and discovered X-rays in Würzburg in Nov 1895 while working with a cathode-ray tube; nothing newer affects this.

explanation: Röntgen called the mysterious rays X-rays because he did not know what they were, and in many languages they still carry his name.

question: In 1859, young chemist Robert Chesebrough visited the Pennsylvania oil fields and saw workers smearing a gooey residue scraped from the drilling rigs onto their cuts and burns. Which product did he refine from it?
source_excerpt: if it was rubbed on an injury, then it would lessen the pain and make the injury heal quicker.

extra.why_interesting: A bathroom-cabinet staple turns out to be a nuisance by-product scraped off oil drilling rigs.
extra.verification_notes: Chesebrough refined Pennsylvania oil-rig rod wax into Vaseline (petroleum jelly), consistent with Wikipedia; the 1859 visit date matches other sources, though Wikipedia gives no date.

explanation: Chesebrough purified the rig residue into petroleum jelly and reportedly ate a spoonful every day to prove its safety, living to 96.

question: In 1964, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson could not get rid of a faint hiss picked up by their horn antenna in New Jersey, which turned out to be the afterglow of the Big Bang. What did they first blame and scrub out of the antenna?
source_excerpt: removing some pigeons nesting in the antenna and cleaning out the accumulated droppings, the noise remained.

extra.why_interesting: The echo of the Big Bang was nearly dismissed as a bird problem, a lovely collision of the cosmic and the mundane.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms they removed nesting pigeons and cleaned out droppings but the noise remained; observations began in 1964.

explanation: They evicted the pigeons and cleaned out what Penzias politely called white dielectric material, but the hiss stayed and earned them the 1978 Nobel Prize.

question: Thomas Edison is remembered for the phonograph, the practical light bulb and the motion-picture camera. Roughly how many US patents were granted in his name?
source_excerpt: Edison held 1,093 U.S. patents and an additional 1,239 foreign patents

extra.why_interesting: Players know Edison for three or four famous inventions and underestimate the industrial scale of his patent output.
extra.verification_notes: Edison held 1,093 US patents, matching 'About 1,000' and clearly distinct from the other options; see https://edison.rutgers.edu/research/edison-s-patents

explanation: Edison held 1,093 US patents, a record that stood for decades, thanks to a research factory at Menlo Park that churned out inventions on an industrial schedule.

question: In 1879, chemist Constantin Fahlberg went home from his coal-tar experiments without washing his hands and found his bread at dinner tasted strangely sweet. Which artificial sweetener had he stumbled on?
source_excerpt: Fahlberg noticed a sweet taste on his hand one evening and connected it to benzoic sulfimide, the compound he had been working with that day.

extra.why_interesting: The first artificial sweetener was found by poor lab hygiene, not by looking for sugar substitutes.
extra.verification_notes: Fahlberg discovered saccharin in 1879 in Remsen's Johns Hopkins lab while working on coal-tar derivatives, and the bread anecdote is the standard account, though some tellings say he tasted it on his hand.

explanation: Fahlberg rushed back to the lab and tasted every beaker on his bench until he found the sweet one, then patented saccharin without crediting his supervisor Ira Remsen.

question: In 1669, Hamburg alchemist Hennig Brand boiled down enormous quantities of human urine hoping to find gold, and instead isolated a waxy substance that glowed in the dark. Which chemical element had he discovered?
source_excerpt: accidentally discovered the chemical element phosphorus while searching for the 'philosopher's stone', a substance which was believed to transmute base metals into gold.

extra.why_interesting: The glow clue gives a path, and the player is startled that a chemical element came out of a bucket of urine.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms Brand discovered phosphorus around 1669 in Hamburg by boiling down urine while seeking the philosopher's stone, and that it glowed.

explanation: Brand's glowing residue was phosphorus, the first element discovered since ancient times, and its name means light-bearer in Greek.

question: In 1856, 18-year-old chemist William Perkin was trying to make a synthetic version of a malaria drug from coal tar and instead produced mauveine, the world's first synthetic dye. Which malaria drug was he chasing?
source_excerpt: Perkin attempted to synthesize quinine, an expensive natural substance needed to treat malaria.

extra.why_interesting: The entire synthetic dye industry began as a failed attempt at a malaria cure, and the malaria clue gives a fair route to the answer.
extra.verification_notes: Perkin, aged 18 in 1856, was trying to synthesize quinine when he discovered mauveine; the 'first synthetic dye' wording is a minor simplification of 'first commercial synthetic organic dye'.

explanation: Quinine still had to be extracted from cinchona bark, so a cheap synthetic version would have been a fortune, but Perkin's purple accident made him rich instead.

question: An engineer at the radar company Raytheon noticed that the chocolate bar in his pocket had melted while he stood near a working radar set — the moment that gave us the microwave oven. In which decade did it happen?
source_excerpt: Raytheon filed the patent application on October 8, 1945, for a microwave cooking oven.

extra.why_interesting: Most people place the microwave oven in the 1960s or 1970s, when it reached ordinary kitchens. The radar clue is a foothold toward wartime, so the answer feels like an 'of course' rather than a lucky guess — and the payoff is a first model the size of a wardrobe.
extra.verification_notes: Spencer's microwave oven patent was filed in October 1945, so the 1940s is correct; the melted-bar story is legend, but the decade is unaffected (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Spencer).

explanation: Percy Spencer made the discovery in 1945, and Raytheon's first commercial Radarange went on sale in 1947. That first oven stood about 1.8 metres tall and weighed roughly 340 kilograms, so it went into restaurant and ship kitchens, not homes.

question: Doctor Who first aired on the BBC on 23 November 1963, overshadowed by news of which event the day before?
source_excerpt: eighty seconds later than the scheduled programme time, because of announcements concerning the previous day's assassination of John F. Kennedy.

extra.why_interesting: A beloved sci-fi institution debuted while the world was in shock, and the date given lets players reason their way to the answer.
extra.verification_notes: Doctor Who premiered 23 Nov 1963, delayed by announcements about JFK's assassination the previous day (22 Nov); confirmed on Wikipedia https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_Who.

explanation: President Kennedy was shot in Dallas on 22 November 1963, and the BBC repeated the opening episode a week later because so few had noticed it.

question: The Sopranos ended in 2007 with a sudden cut to black while which Journey song played on the diner jukebox?
source_excerpt: The use of an abrupt cut to black followed by several seconds of silence led many viewers to initially believe that their cable or DVR had cut out

extra.why_interesting: The cut to black is the famous part; the song that made the scene is the proud-recall detail.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's page for the finale 'Made in America' confirms Journey's 'Don't Stop Believin'' plays in the diner before the cut to black on June 10, 2007.

explanation: Many viewers thought their TV had broken, and the 1981 song enjoyed a huge sales revival after the episode.

question: In The Simpsons, which male member of the central family is voiced by a woman?
source_excerpt: She is known for her long-running role as Bart Simpson on the animated television series The Simpsons.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the voice of a mischievous boy and rarely imagine it belongs to an adult woman.
extra.verification_notes: Nancy Cartwright voices Bart, the only male member of the central Simpson family voiced by a woman; no recasting found (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bart_Simpson).

explanation: Nancy Cartwright has voiced Bart since 1987, and she originally auditioned for Lisa.

question: Over its six seasons, how many different actresses played Queen Elizabeth II in The Crown?
source_excerpt: Seasons 1-2: Claire Foy; Seasons 3-4: Olivia Colman; Seasons 5-6: Imelda Staunton

extra.why_interesting: Players remember the recasting but have to reason through the decades to land on the right count.
extra.verification_notes: Foy, Colman and Staunton each played the Queen across six seasons; Viola Prettejohn's teenage Princess Elizabeth flashback role is the only minor ambiguity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crown_(TV_series)).

explanation: Claire Foy, Olivia Colman and Imelda Staunton each took two seasons, ageing the queen from the 1940s to the 2000s.

question: The reality format Big Brother, named after Orwell's all-seeing ruler, was first broadcast in 1999 in which country?
source_excerpt: The first version of Big Brother was broadcast in 1999 on Veronica in the Netherlands

extra.why_interesting: Most players assume the format is American or British; it came from a small Dutch broadcaster before conquering the world.
extra.verification_notes: Big Brother first aired in 1999 on Veronica in the Netherlands, per Wikipedia's franchise article.

explanation: Producer John de Mol launched it on the Dutch channel Veronica, and within a few years it was airing in dozens of countries.

question: Which walled Croatian city stood in for King's Landing in Game of Thrones?
source_excerpt: the city of Dubrovnik and nearby locations allowed exterior shots of a walled, coastal medieval city

extra.why_interesting: A real medieval city doubled as the fantasy capital, and tourism there boomed as a result.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Game of Thrones article confirms Dubrovnik's walls and Fort Lovrijenac were used for King's Landing, and nothing newer contradicts it.

explanation: Its old town walls and Adriatic setting matched the capital so well that the city now limits daily tourist numbers.

question: John Cleese's Fawlty Towers is regularly voted the best British sitcom ever. How many episodes were made in total?
source_excerpt: Total of 12 episodes across 2 series (6 episodes each). Series 1 aired in 1975, Series 2 in 1979.

extra.why_interesting: The show's reputation is enormous, so players expect dozens of episodes; the whole legacy rests on a dozen.
extra.verification_notes: Fawlty Towers has 12 TV episodes (two series of six); the cancelled TV revival and stage sequels don't change that, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fawlty_Towers

explanation: Two series of six episodes each, aired in 1975 and 1979, and Cleese refused to make more for fear of spoiling it.

question: In Seinfeld, Jerry's neighbour Kramer is almost always called by his surname. What is his first name?
source_excerpt: George finds out his first name of 'Cosmo' through an encounter with Kramer's long-estranged mother, Babs, in 'The Switch.'

extra.why_interesting: A main character went six seasons without a first name, and the reveal became a running joke.
extra.verification_notes: Kramer's first name is Cosmo, revealed in 'The Switch'; the 'Conrad' alternative came from an unproduced episode only (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmo_Kramer).

explanation: It stayed secret for six seasons until his mother let it slip in the episode 'The Switch'.

question: In which year was the very first Eurovision Song Contest broadcast?
source_excerpt: The inaugural Eurovision Song Contest took place on May 24, 1956, in Lugano, Switzerland, specifically at the Teatro Kursaal venue.

extra.why_interesting: Players know it is old but tend to place it in the colour-TV era; it predates most households owning a set.
extra.verification_notes: The first Eurovision Song Contest took place on 24 May 1956 in Lugano, Switzerland, so 1956 is correct.

explanation: Seven countries met in Lugano, Switzerland, in 1956, and the host nation won with Lys Assia.

question: Which country produced Squid Game, the most-watched series in Netflix's history?
source_excerpt: It became Netflix's most-watched series and received numerous accolades, including six Primetime Emmy Awards and one Golden Globe.

extra.why_interesting: A non-English series became the biggest hit of the world's largest streamer, a milestone worth marking.
extra.verification_notes: Squid Game is a South Korean production and remains Netflix's most-watched series (S1 265.2M views, ahead of Wednesday S1) per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Squid_Game.

explanation: Its 2021 debut proved a non-English show could top the charts worldwide, and the green tracksuits became a global costume.

question: Psychiatrist Frasier Crane got his own hit sitcom in 1993, but he first appeared as a bar regular in which earlier series?
source_excerpt: debuted in the Cheers third-season premiere, 'Rebound (Part 1)' (1984), as Diane Chambers' love interest

extra.why_interesting: The spin-off became bigger than many remember the parent being, so players enjoy connecting the two.
extra.verification_notes: Frasier Crane debuted in Cheers season 3 (1984) and the spin-off Frasier premiered in September 1993; no newer event changes this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frasier_Crane).

explanation: He joined the Boston bar in 1984, and his spin-off went on to win a then-record 37 Emmy Awards.

question: In 1980 the whole world was asking 'Who shot J.R.?'. Which TV series was it about?
source_excerpt: 'Who shot J.R.?' is an advertising catchphrase created in 1980 by American network CBS to promote the prime time television soap opera Dallas.

extra.why_interesting: The phrase outlived the show; many know the question without instantly placing the series.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms 'Who shot J.R.?' was a 1980 CBS promotional catchphrase for the soap opera Dallas.

explanation: The reveal episode drew an estimated 350 million viewers worldwide, and the shooter was his sister-in-law Kristin.

question: Which animated family made their TV debut in 1987 as short filler cartoons on a comedian's sketch show, two years before getting their own series?
topic: Television, series and famous TV moments
source_excerpt: The shorts first aired on April 19, 1987, starting with 'Good Night.'

extra.why_interesting: Players picture the Simpsons as a show that was always a flagship; the surprise is that they began as throwaway filler between someone else's sketches.
extra.verification_notes: The Simpsons shorts debuted on The Tracey Ullman Show on April 19, 1987, and the series premiered on December 17, 1989; "two years" is a loose but acceptable rounding (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Simpsons_shorts).

explanation: The yellow family started as brief bumpers on The Tracey Ullman Show, and the standalone series that launched in December 1989 went on to become the longest-running scripted primetime show in American television.

question: Rowan Atkinson's Mr. Bean has been rerun around the world for more than three decades. Roughly how many original episodes of the live-action TV series were actually made?
topic: Television, series and famous TV moments
source_excerpt: The series originally aired on ITV, beginning with the pilot episode on 1 January 1990 and ending with 'Goodnight Mr. Bean' on 31 October 1995.

extra.why_interesting: Because Mr. Bean has been in constant reruns on channels in nearly every country for thirty years, players assume there is a huge back catalogue; the real number is tiny.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the live-action series had 14 episodes plus one special (1990-1995), so 'Fewer than 20' is correct and no newer live-action episodes were found.

explanation: Only 15 episodes were made between 1990 and 1995, and because Bean almost never speaks, that handful of half-hours travelled to broadcasters in nearly every country without needing dubbing.

question: Christmas is always on 25 December, but the fasting month of Ramadan begins roughly eleven days earlier each year, drifting through all four seasons over about three decades. Why does it move like this?
correct_answer: Islamic calendar is purely lunar, no leap months
alternative_answers: Lunar year is shorter than solar year
Twelve moon months are only 354 days
Months follow the moon, not the sun
No extra month is added to realign with the seasons
headline_answer: Islamic calendar is purely lunar, no leap months
topic: Holidays, festivals and traditions around the world
source_excerpt: months of the Hijri calendar advance about eleven days earlier each year, relative to the equinoxes

extra.verification_notes: The Islamic calendar is purely lunar (354/355-day years) with intercalation prohibited, so Ramadan drifts about 11 days earlier per year and cycles through the seasons in about 33 years (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_calendar).

explanation: The Islamic calendar is strictly lunar: each month begins with the new crescent moon, and twelve lunar months add up to about 354 days. That is roughly eleven days shorter than the 365-day solar year the Gregorian calendar follows. Many other lunar-based systems, such as the Chinese or Hebrew calendars, periodically insert an extra 'leap' month to stay aligned with the seasons, but the Islamic calendar never does. So Ramadan, and every other Islamic date, slides about eleven days earlier each Gregorian year and completes a full tour of the seasons in roughly 33 years.

question: In Japan, Christmas dinner for millions of families comes from one American fast-food chain, and the Christmas buckets are often pre-ordered weeks in advance. Which chain?
source_excerpt: Eating KFC food as a Christmas time meal has since become a widely practiced custom in Japan.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture Christmas dinner as roast turkey or goose; Japan's answer is an American fast-food bucket ordered weeks in advance.
extra.verification_notes: KFC's Christmas bucket tradition in Japan, with pre-ordering, is well documented and still current per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/KFC_in_Japan.

explanation: A 1974 campaign called 'Kentucky for Christmas' turned the fried-chicken chain into a Japanese holiday ritual, and Christmas Eve is now its busiest day of the year there.

question: At the stroke of midnight on New Year's Eve, people all over Spain race to eat twelve small pieces of fruit, one on each chime of the clock, for luck in the twelve months ahead. Which fruit?
source_excerpt: Tradition has it that you have to eat them one by one, in time with the striking of the clock at midnight on 31 December.

extra.why_interesting: Twelve items in twelve seconds sounds like a stunt, not a national custom; the fruit turns out to be the humblest thing on the table.
extra.verification_notes: Spain's Nochevieja tradition is eating twelve grapes (uvas de la suerte), one per clock chime, for luck in the twelve months ahead; no newer event affects this.

explanation: They are the 'twelve grapes of luck', and the whole country watches the clock on Madrid's Puerta del Sol to time each bite, which is harder than it sounds with a mouth full of grapes.

question: True or false: Cinco de Mayo, the fifth of May, is Mexico's Independence Day.
source_excerpt: Cinco de Mayo is sometimes mistaken for Mexican Independence Day—the most important national holiday in Mexico—which is celebrated on September 16.

extra.why_interesting: Many people, especially in the US, assume the big May party is Mexico's independence day; it actually marks a single battle against the French, fought decades after independence.
extra.verification_notes: Cinco de Mayo commemorates the 1862 Battle of Puebla; Mexican Independence Day is September 16, so 'False' is correct (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinco_de_Mayo).

explanation: The fifth of May marks an 1862 victory over an invading French army at the Battle of Puebla, while Mexico celebrates independence on the sixteenth of September.

question: Munich's Oktoberfest began in 1810 as a public party thrown for a royal wedding, and the field where it is still held is called the Theresienwiese. What was Therese's role at that very first festival?
source_excerpt: The site was named Theresienwiese ('Therese's Meadow') the following year and is still called Wiesn.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the beer tents but not that the ground beneath them is named for a woman; once the stem says 'wedding', the answer clicks into place.
extra.verification_notes: Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen was the bride of Crown Prince Ludwig in 1810, and the Theresienwiese is named for her (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oktoberfest).

explanation: Princess Therese of Saxe-Hildburghausen married Crown Prince Ludwig, later King Ludwig I of Bavaria, and the meadow where Munich celebrated has carried her name ever since.

question: On New Year's Eve, Buddhist temples across Japan ring their great bells a fixed number of times, one ring for each worldly desire that Buddhism says troubles a human being. How many rings?
source_excerpt: Most temples ring the bell 108 times at midnight on December 31st as part of New Year's Eve celebrations in Japan.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect a round number like twelve or a hundred; the odd total makes sense only once you know the Buddhist count of human weaknesses.
extra.verification_notes: Joya no Kane tradition: temples ring the bell 108 times, once per worldly desire (klesha); some split it 107 before and 1 after midnight, which doesn't change the total (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joya_no_Kane).

explanation: The ritual is called joya no kane, and the same number of 108 shows up in the beads of a Buddhist prayer necklace, so the last ring is meant to leave the listener clean for the new year.

question: The carved Halloween lantern comes from Ireland and Scotland, but the pumpkin does not. Before emigrants discovered pumpkins in America, which root vegetable did they hollow out and carve into scary faces?
source_excerpt: turnips or mangel wurzels, hollowed out to act as lanterns and often carved with grotesque faces

extra.why_interesting: The pumpkin feels ancient and essential, but it is a North American substitute; the original was a far smaller, uglier root from the Irish kitchen.
extra.verification_notes: Turnips were the traditional jack-o'-lantern vegetable in Ireland and Scotland before pumpkins; mangel wurzels were also used, but turnip is the canonical answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack-o'-lantern).

explanation: Carving a hard little turnip was slow and painful work, so when Irish immigrants met the big, soft American pumpkin they switched almost immediately, and the pumpkin lantern travelled back across the Atlantic.

question: Mongolia's national festival, Naadam, is built around the 'three games of men'. Two of them are wrestling and archery. What is the third sport?
source_excerpt: The three standard sports of wrestling, horse racing, and archery are recorded in the 13th-century book The Secret History of the Mongols.

extra.why_interesting: Two of the three sports are given, and the third is obvious the moment the player remembers what Mongolia is famous for.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the three games of men are wrestling, horse racing and archery, with no changes found.

explanation: The races are ridden over open steppe for tens of kilometres, and the jockeys are mostly children as young as five, because lighter riders mean faster horses.

question: Pamplona's running of the bulls was a local Spanish festival until a 1926 novel made it world famous, and the city later put up a statue of the author outside the bullring. Which American writer?
source_excerpt: To Ernest Hemingway, Nobel Prize in Literature, friend of this town and admirer of its festivals, which he knew how to discover and promote.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the bull run has always drawn global crowds; in fact a single American novelist put it on the map, and the city still thanks him with a statue.
extra.verification_notes: Pamplona's official tourism site confirms the 1968 Hemingway monument beside the bullring; The Sun Also Rises (1926) popularized the festival.

explanation: The novel is 'The Sun Also Rises', known as 'Fiesta' in Europe, and Hemingway kept coming back to San Fermín for decades, so the week in July became a pilgrimage for his readers.

question: China's Mid-Autumn Festival is celebrated under the brightest full moon of the year, and families share a round, dense pastry that takes its name from that night sky. What is the pastry called?
source_excerpt: A mooncake is a Chinese baked item traditionally eaten during the Mid-Autumn Festival.

extra.why_interesting: The pastry is named after the thing the festival celebrates, so a player who knows the festival's timing can reason to it even without having tasted one.
extra.verification_notes: Mooncake (月餅, 'moon cake') is the round, dense pastry traditionally eaten at Mid-Autumn Festival, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mooncake.

explanation: A traditional mooncake is small but packed with lotus-seed paste and often a salted egg yolk standing in for the full moon, and the fancy gift boxes have become a status symbol.

question: Every August the Spanish town of Buñol holds La Tomatina, an hour-long street fight using overripe tomatoes trucked in for about twenty thousand participants. Roughly how much tomato is thrown in a typical year?
source_excerpt: In 2015, it was estimated that almost 145,000 kg (320,000 lb) of tomatoes were thrown.

extra.why_interesting: Players picture a few crates of tomatoes; the real supply arrives in a convoy of trucks, and the scale is what makes the hour-long fight possible.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia reports about 145 tonnes thrown in 2015 with 20,000 ticket holders, so 100 tonnes is the nearest order-of-magnitude option.

explanation: Around 120 to 150 tonnes arrive in a convoy of trucks, the streets end up ankle-deep in pulp, and the acid in the tomatoes leaves the stone pavements cleaner than before the fight.

question: The New Year's Eve ball drop in New York's Times Square is watched by a billion people on screens today, but the very first ball, made of iron and wood and lit by one hundred light bulbs, was lowered in which year?
topic: New Year's Eve in Times Square
source_excerpt: built from iron and wood, illuminated by a hundred incandescent light bulbs, weighed 700 pounds (320 kg), and measured 5 feet (1.5 m) in diameter.

extra.why_interesting: The ball drop feels like a product of the television era, but it predates radio broadcasting, and the first ball was an iron-and-wood sphere lit with a hundred bulbs.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the first iron-and-wood ball with 100 bulbs dropped Dec 31, 1907 (welcoming 1908); no newer development changes this.

explanation: The first drop on 31 December 1907 welcomed in 1908, long before radio or television existed, and it was introduced because the city had banned the fireworks used in earlier Times Square celebrations.

question: Munich's Oktoberfest, the world's biggest beer festival, officially opens in which month of the year?
topic: Holidays, festivals and traditions around the world
source_excerpt: Oktoberfest has typically lasted 16 days, starting on the first Saturday after 15 September and ending on the first Sunday in October.

extra.why_interesting: The name screams October, so the player assumes the whole thing happens then — but the bulk of the beer tents are open in September, with only the final few days spilling into the month it is named after.
extra.verification_notes: Oktoberfest opens in September under a standing rule (first Saturday after 15 September); 2026 ran Sept 19 to Oct 4, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oktoberfest.

explanation: Since 1872 the festival has started in late September to catch warmer weather, so most of its sixteen-odd days are over before October even begins.

question: At Zurich's spring festival Sechseläuten, a snowman effigy packed with fireworks is set alight, and the time it takes for its head to explode is said to forecast what?
alternative_answers: how good the summer will be
the weather of the coming summer
topic: Holidays, festivals and traditions around the world
source_excerpt: a quick explosion promises a warm, sunny summer, a drawn-out burning indicates a cold and rainy one.

extra.why_interesting: The player pictures a festive bonfire and assumes it is just a party; the twist is that the exploding snowman is treated as a weather oracle, and the clue 'spring festival' plus 'snowman' gives a reasoning path to 'summer weather'.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Böögg's head explosion time is the traditional forecast of the coming summer's weather: a quick burst means a warm summer, a slow one a cold, rainy summer.

explanation: A quick explosion promises a warm, sunny summer, while a slow burn supposedly means a cold and rainy one, and the whole city watches the clock.

question: Every Christmas Eve at three in the afternoon, millions of Swedes stop everything to watch the same 1958 Disney television special, broadcast almost unchanged since 1959. Which cartoon character headlines it?
topic: Holidays, festivals and traditions around the world
source_excerpt: In Sweden, the program is titled "Kalle Anka och hans vänner önskar God Jul" (Donald Duck and His Friends Wish You a Merry Christmas).

extra.why_interesting: Players assume Christmas Eve centrepieces are hymns, mass or a royal speech; in Sweden the nation stops for an American cartoon duck in a show that has barely changed in over sixty years.
extra.verification_notes: The Swedish tradition is titled 'Kalle Anka (Donald Duck) och hans vänner önskar God Jul'; Jiminy Cricket is the original US host, which creates only a slight ambiguity (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/From_All_of_Us_to_All_of_You).

explanation: The show is known in Sweden as Kalle Anka and his friends wish you a Merry Christmas, and it regularly pulls in around a third of the entire country, making it one of the most-watched programmes of the Swedish year.

question: The Eiffel Tower, built from wrought iron, is measurably taller in July than in January, by roughly the length of a pencil. Why?
alternative_answers: The metal expands when it is hot
Summer temperatures make the structure expand
Metal contracts in the cold and expands in warmth
source_excerpt: the top of the tower may shift away from the sun by up to 18 cm (7 in) due to thermal expansion of the metal

extra.verification_notes: Thermal expansion of the wrought-iron structure makes the tower taller in summer, commonly cited as about 15 cm; no newer developments contradict this (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eiffel_Tower).

explanation: Metals expand when heated and contract when cooled. The tower is made of about 7,300 tonnes of wrought iron, and over roughly 300 metres of height the tiny expansion of every beam adds up. On hot summer days the structure grows by up to about 15 centimetres and shrinks again in winter. The sun also warms one side more than the other, so the top of the tower leans slightly away from the sun during the day.

question: From 1889 the Eiffel Tower was the tallest man-made structure on Earth. In which city was the skyscraper that finally overtook it in 1930?
source_excerpt: In 1930, the tower lost the title of the world's tallest structure when the Chrysler Building in New York City was completed.

extra.why_interesting: Players know the Eiffel Tower is tall but rarely realise it held the world record for four decades; the dethroning city is deducible from the 1930 skyscraper boom.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Eiffel Tower article confirms the Chrysler Building in New York City overtook the Eiffel Tower in 1930, and a historical fact like this can't be made stale by later events.

explanation: The Chrysler Building took the record in 1930, only to lose it to the Empire State Building a year later.

question: Two 88-storey twin towers linked by a double-decker skybridge were the world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004. Which capital city are they in?
source_excerpt: a double decker skybridge connecting the two towers on the 41st and 42nd floors

extra.why_interesting: Many players picture the twin towers but place them in the wrong Asian city; the skybridge detail is the foothold that identifies them.
extra.verification_notes: Petronas Towers (88 storeys, double-decker skybridge, tallest 1998–2004) are in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia's capital, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petronas_Towers

explanation: The Petronas Towers' skybridge isn't bolted to either tower; it sits on sliding bearings so the two towers can sway independently in the wind.

question: The Golden Gate Bridge is painted a reddish orange and contains no gold at all. What does the 'Golden Gate' in its name actually refer to?
alternative_answers: The entrance to San Francisco Bay
source_excerpt: the Golden Gate, the one-mile-wide (1.6 km) strait connecting San Francisco Bay and the Pacific Ocean

extra.why_interesting: Nearly everyone assumes the name describes the bridge itself, and is puzzled by its orange colour; the answer reveals the name predates the bridge entirely.
extra.verification_notes: The bridge is named after the Golden Gate strait it spans, and it is painted international orange with no gold, per Wikipedia.

explanation: Explorer John C. Fremont named the entrance to San Francisco Bay the Golden Gate in 1846, nearly a century before the bridge opened in 1937.

question: In 1968 the City of London sold its 19th-century London Bridge to an American businessman, who shipped it across the Atlantic and rebuilt it stone by stone. In which US state does it stand today?
source_excerpt: The Arizona bridge is a reinforced concrete structure clad in the original masonry of the 1830s bridge.

extra.why_interesting: A London landmark standing in the American desert is delightful in itself; the player who knows the story gets a payoff, and others can take a sporting guess at a US state.
extra.verification_notes: The 1830s London Bridge was sold in 1968 to Robert McCulloch and stands in Lake Havasu City, Arizona; the article mentions no relocation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Bridge_(Lake_Havasu_City)).

explanation: Robert McCulloch rebuilt it over a man-made channel at Lake Havasu City in the Arizona desert, where it reopened in 1971.

question: Built around 126 AD, which Roman building still holds the record for the world's largest dome made of unreinforced concrete?
source_excerpt: Almost two thousand years after it was built, the Pantheon's dome is still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume concrete records belong to modern engineering; a Roman building holding one nearly two thousand years later is the surprise, and 'Roman dome' narrows it to one famous candidate.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Pantheon (c. 126 AD, Hadrian) still has the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome; I did not search for newer challengers.

explanation: Its 43-metre dome gets lighter towards the top, with pumice mixed into the concrete, and is crowned by an open hole that lets rain fall straight onto the floor.

question: Opened in 1994, which tunnel holds the record for the longest stretch of any tunnel running beneath the sea, about 38 kilometres of it?
source_excerpt: the longest underwater section of any tunnel in the world, at 37.9 km (23.5 miles)

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the record for undersea tunnelling belongs to Japan or to some newer mega-project; the 1994 date and the sea clue steer them to a tunnel they already know, which turns out to hold the record outright.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the Channel Tunnel opened in 1994 and has the world's longest undersea section at 37.9 km, with no newer tunnel exceeding it.

explanation: Japan's Seikan Tunnel is longer overall, but the Channel Tunnel has the longest undersea section ever built, roughly 38 kilometres between Folkestone and Coquelles.

question: Japan's Akashi Kaikyō Bridge, the longest suspension span in the world when it opened in 1998, ended up about one metre longer than its blueprints. What stretched it while it was still being built?
source_excerpt: the central span had to be increased by 1 m (3.3 ft).

extra.why_interesting: Players assume a bridge ends up longer because engineers changed the plans; the idea that the ground itself moved the finished towers apart is a shock, yet 'Japan' plus 'stretched' gives a thinking player a real route to the answer.
extra.verification_notes: The 1995 Kobe earthquake moved the towers during construction, adding 1 m to the central span; the 2022 Çanakkale record doesn't affect the past-tense 'when it opened' claim (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akashi_Kaikyō_Bridge).

explanation: The 1995 Kobe earthquake shifted the already-built towers apart, so the engineers simply adjusted the design to the new, slightly longer span.

question: Opened in 2004 and designed with architect Norman Foster, which cable-stayed motorway bridge in southern France rises higher at its tallest point than the Eiffel Tower?
source_excerpt: 13 m taller than the 330-metre Eiffel Tower

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the Eiffel Tower is the tallest structure France has ever built; the overturn is that a motorway bridge in a rural valley quietly tops it, and the Norman Foster and 2004 footholds give a motivated player a real route to the name.
extra.verification_notes: Millau Viaduct opened Dec 2004, Foster-designed, cable-stayed, 343 m pylon vs Eiffel Tower 330 m; losing the world's-tallest-bridge title in 2025 doesn't affect the question's claims (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Millau_Viaduct).

explanation: Its tallest mast reaches about 343 metres above the base, a little over the roughly 330 metres of the Eiffel Tower, as it carries the A75 motorway across the Tarn valley.

question: True or false: you can tell how old a ladybird is by counting its spots.
source_excerpt: The number of spots on a ladybird indicates what species it belongs to, not, as commonly believed, how old it is.

extra.why_interesting: The childhood 'count the spots to find its age' story is everywhere; the number is a species badge, not a birthday counter.
extra.verification_notes: Spot count is fixed at adult emergence and indicates species, not age, so 'False' is correct (https://www.lovethegarden.com/uk-en/article/11-fascinating-ladybird-facts).

explanation: The spots are fixed by species, so a seven-spot ladybird has seven from the day it emerges until it dies about a year later.

question: Each autumn, monarch butterflies fly thousands of kilometres from Canada and the United States to spend the winter clustered in the mountain forests of which country?
source_excerpt: The population east of the Rocky Mountains attempts to migrate to the sanctuaries of the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve in the Mexican state of Michoacán

extra.why_interesting: A paper-thin insect completing a continental migration to one small patch of mountain forest is astonishing even though the destination is well known.
extra.verification_notes: Eastern North American monarchs overwinter in the oyamel fir mountain forests of Michoacán, Mexico; the California coastal population does not make the question ambiguous.

explanation: Millions of them pack onto fir trees in the mountains of central Mexico so densely that the branches sag under butterfly weight.

question: Only female mosquitoes bite. What do the males feed on instead?
source_excerpt: Both male and female mosquitoes feed on nectar, aphid honeydew, and plant juices

extra.why_interesting: Players think of mosquitoes as blood-drinkers by definition; half of them are harmless flower visitors.
extra.verification_notes: Male mosquitoes feed on nectar and other plant sugars; only females blood-feed, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosquito.

explanation: Males live on nectar and plant sugars, and the females only need blood for the protein to make their eggs.

question: Mayflies spend a year or more growing underwater as nymphs, but once they take to the air, the adult of a typical species lives for roughly how long?
source_excerpt: The lifespan of an adult mayfly is very short, varying with the species.

extra.why_interesting: The contrast between a long hidden youth and a one-day adulthood is the whole insect's story.
extra.verification_notes: Adult mayflies typically live from under an hour to about a day depending on species, so 'about one day' is the standard accepted answer; nymphs last months to years per Wikipedia.

explanation: Adult mayflies have no working mouthparts, so they emerge, mate, lay eggs and die within about a day, some species within a few hours.

question: Despite their name, fireflies are not flies at all. Which major insect group do they actually belong to?
source_excerpt: The Lampyridae are a family of elateroid beetles with more than 2,400 described species, many of which are light-emitting.

extra.why_interesting: The common name points the player straight at flies; the answer is a group they would never have guessed glows.
extra.verification_notes: Fireflies (Lampyridae) are beetles in order Coleoptera, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firefly.

explanation: Fireflies are soft-bodied beetles, and the glowing larvae we call glow-worms are beetle grubs too.

question: Leafcutter ants carry huge pieces of leaf back to their nests, yet they never eat them. What do they use the leaves for?
source_excerpt: cut and process fresh vegetation (leaves, flowers, and grasses) to serve as the nutritional substrate for their fungal cultivates.

extra.why_interesting: The famous picture of ants carrying leaf pieces looks like a food run; the leaves are actually fertiliser for an underground crop.
extra.verification_notes: Leafcutter ants use cut leaves as substrate to cultivate a fungus that feeds the colony; the 'never eat them' wording is slightly loose (adults drink leaf sap) but doesn't affect the answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leafcutter_ant).

explanation: They chew the leaves into a mulch to feed underground fungus gardens, and that fungus is what the colony actually eats.

question: The red colouring carmine, listed on European labels as E120 and found in sweets, yoghurts and lipstick, is made by crushing what?
source_excerpt: The pigment is produced from carminic acid, which is extracted from some scale insects such as the cochineal scale.

extra.why_interesting: A colour people eat in sweets and wear as lipstick comes from an animal source nobody expects on an ingredient list.
extra.verification_notes: Carmine (E120) is produced from cochineal scale insects, and no newer development changes this per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmine

explanation: It comes from dried cochineal insects, tiny scale bugs harvested from cacti in Latin America, and it takes tens of thousands of them to make a kilogram of dye.

question: A silk cocoon is unwound into one single, unbroken thread. Roughly how long is the thread from just one cocoon?
source_excerpt: The cocoon is made of one continuous white or yellow strand of silk averaging about 915 metres (1,000 yards) long.

extra.why_interesting: A cocoon fits in your palm, so a thread the length of a long city street feels impossible until you remember how fine silk is.
extra.verification_notes: A Bombyx mori cocoon is a single continuous thread of roughly 300–900+ m (avg ~915 m), so ~1 km is the closest option (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombyx_mori).

explanation: The filament usually runs 600 to 900 metres, which is why a single kimono can take thousands of cocoons.

question: A dragonfly may live for several years, yet it spends only a few weeks as the flying insect we recognise. Where does it spend all the rest of that time?
alternative_answers: At the bottom of a pond
source_excerpt: The nymph stage of dragonflies lasts up to five years in large species, and between two months and three years in smaller species.

extra.why_interesting: The glittering flier over the pond is the brief final chapter; the real life of a dragonfly is as a predator crawling on the pond bottom.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the nymph stage lasts up to five years underwater while most adults live five weeks or less.

explanation: It lives as a nymph on the bottom of ponds and streams, hunting tadpoles and even small fish, before crawling out to split its skin and fly.

question: In 2007 a European experiment exposed living animals directly to the vacuum of space, and some survived and later reproduced. Which tiny eight-legged creature, often found in garden moss, did it?
source_excerpt: four pairs of legs, each ending in claws

extra.why_interesting: Players picture astronauts in suits; the first animal to survive naked in open space was a half-millimetre creature from garden moss.
extra.verification_notes: The 2007 FOTON-M3 experiment exposed tardigrades to space vacuum, some survived and reproduced; they have eight legs and live in moss (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tardigrade).

explanation: Tardigrades, also called water bears, can dry out into a dormant state that shrugs off vacuum, freezing and heavy radiation, then revive with a drop of water.

question: A cricket is famous for its chirping, and it listens for rivals and mates with a pair of ears. On which part of its body are those ears?
source_excerpt: The tibiae of the front legs bear one or more tympani which are used for the reception of sound.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone knows crickets are famous for sound, so it is a jolt to learn their ears are nowhere near their heads.
extra.verification_notes: Crickets' tympanal ears are on the tibiae of the front legs, per Wikipedia (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cricket_(insect)).

explanation: Tiny eardrums sit on the shins of the front legs, so a cricket effectively hears through its knees.

question: A butterfly can tell whether a plant is good for its eggs just by landing on it. Which part of its body does the tasting?
source_excerpt: Butterflies taste with their feet using chemoreceptors on their tarsi, which help them find food and select egg-laying sites.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume tasting happens in the mouth; discovering that a butterfly samples a leaf simply by landing on it is a small, delightful shock.
extra.verification_notes: Butterflies have tarsal chemoreceptors on their feet that they use to taste leaves and judge host plants before laying eggs; no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: Butterflies carry taste sensors on their feet, so a quick touchdown on a leaf tells them whether a caterpillar could feed there.

question: Periodical cicadas in North America spend years underground, then emerge in vast swarms every 13 years or every 17 years. What do those two numbers have in common mathematically?
source_excerpt: Both 13 and 17 are prime numbers—integers greater than one divisible only by themselves and one.

extra.why_interesting: The player expects a biology answer and instead finds mathematics hiding in the life cycle of a bug: both numbers are prime, and that is no accident.
extra.verification_notes: 13 and 17 are both prime numbers, as stated in the Wikipedia article on periodical cicadas; I found no newer developments that change this.

explanation: Prime cycles make it almost impossible for predators with shorter life cycles to fall into step with the cicadas, so the swarms rarely meet a well-prepared enemy.

question: Meganeura was a dragonfly-like insect that flew over the coal forests about 300 million years ago, long before the first dinosaurs. Roughly how wide was its wingspan?
source_excerpt: a wingspan about 65–75 cm (2.13–2.46 ft)

extra.why_interesting: Players know dragonflies as palm-sized; the idea of one the size of a large bird of prey, flying over coal forests long before dinosaurs, is hard to believe yet well documented.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia gives Meganeura monyi a wingspan of about 65–75 cm from the Late Carboniferous (~300 Ma), which matches 'about 70 cm'.

explanation: Meganeura's wings spanned about 70 centimetres, roughly the size of a large hawk, a giant made possible by the oxygen-rich air of the Carboniferous period.

question: The word 'tsunami', used worldwide for a giant sea wave, comes from which language?
source_excerpt: The term 'tsunami' is a borrowing from the Japanese tsunami (津波), meaning 'harbour wave.'

extra.why_interesting: The word is used worldwide and feels international; the payoff is that it literally means 'harbour wave', named by the fishermen who saw their harbours destroyed.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms 'tsunami' is a borrowing from Japanese 津波 ('harbour wave'); this is a fixed etymology that newer events can't change.

explanation: It literally means 'harbour wave', because fishermen out at sea noticed nothing and only found the destruction when they returned to port.

question: The highest air temperature ever reliably recorded on Earth, 56.7 degrees Celsius back in 1913, was measured in which Californian desert valley?
source_excerpt: The highest reliably recorded air temperature is 134.1 °F (56.7 °C), measured on July 10, 1913 at Furnace Creek Ranch in Death Valley, California.

extra.why_interesting: Players expect the record to belong to the Sahara or the Middle East; it actually sits in the United States, and it has stood for over a century.
extra.verification_notes: WMO still recognizes the 56.7 °C reading at Furnace Creek, Death Valley, on 10 July 1913 as the world record; a recent study disputes it, but it has not been decertified.

explanation: The reading was taken at Furnace Creek, and despite all the heatwaves since, no one has officially beaten it in more than a hundred years.

question: The deadliest tropical cyclone ever recorded struck in 1970, killing several hundred thousand people in a low-lying river delta. It hit the territory of which present-day country?
source_excerpt: The 1970 Bhola cyclone... was the deadliest tropical cyclone on record, as well as one of the deadliest humanitarian disasters ever recorded.

extra.why_interesting: Players associate record-breaking storms with the US Gulf Coast or the Caribbean; the deadliest of all struck a river delta on the other side of the world.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 1970 Bhola cyclone is the deadliest tropical cyclone on record (300k-500k deaths), striking East Pakistan, now Bangladesh; I did not separately search for newer events.

explanation: The Bhola cyclone drove a storm surge over the Ganges delta when the area was still East Pakistan, and the slow relief effort helped fuel the war that created Bangladesh a year later.

question: The deadliest natural disaster in United States history was a hurricane in 1900 that flattened an island city on the Texas coast. Which city?
source_excerpt: The Galveston hurricane of 1900 is the deadliest natural disaster to strike the United States.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume Katrina or a San Francisco earthquake is the deadliest US disaster; it was actually a hurricane more than a century ago that flattened an island city few remember.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 1900 Galveston hurricane remains the deadliest natural disaster in US history, with no newer event surpassing it.

explanation: The storm surge swept over the whole island and killed somewhere between six and twelve thousand people, after which the city raised its entire ground level and built a seawall.

question: On All Saints' Day in 1755, while churches were full, an earthquake, a tsunami and fires destroyed most of which European capital city?
source_excerpt: The earthquake struck on the morning of 1 November 1755, All Saints' Day.

extra.why_interesting: Players don't expect a major European capital to have been wiped out by an earthquake and tsunami; the date, with churches packed for a holy day, makes it unforgettable.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the 1 Nov 1755 All Saints' Day earthquake, tsunami and fires destroyed about 85% of Lisbon.

explanation: The disaster shocked Enlightenment Europe, inspired Voltaire's Candide, and led to the city being rebuilt on a grid with some of the first earthquake-resistant buildings.

question: The most powerful earthquake ever recorded by instruments, a magnitude 9.5 in 1960, struck which country?
source_excerpt: the strongest earthquake ever recorded

extra.why_interesting: Players reach for Japan or San Francisco; the strongest quake ever measured hit the long Pacific coast of South America and sent a tsunami across the whole ocean.
extra.verification_notes: The 1960 Valdivia earthquake in Chile is still the strongest instrumentally recorded earthquake (M9.4–9.6, USGS 9.5), and no newer event has surpassed it.

explanation: The Valdivia earthquake sent a tsunami right across the Pacific, killing people in Hawaii and Japan the following day.

question: In 2010, ash from an erupting volcano with an almost unpronounceable name grounded around 100,000 flights across Europe. The volcano is in which country?
source_excerpt: the highest level of air travel disruption since the Second World War

extra.why_interesting: Players remember the chaos but may struggle to place it; the delight is realising a modest eruption on a remote island shut down an entire continent's airspace.
extra.verification_notes: Eyjafjallajökull, whose 2010 eruption caused massive European air disruption, is in Iceland; no newer events change this.

explanation: Eyjafjallajökull was a relatively small eruption, but the fine glassy ash drifting over Europe was considered deadly to jet engines, so the skies stayed empty for nearly a week.

question: Three of these famous volcanoes are in Indonesia. Which one is not?
source_excerpt: Mount Pinatubo is an active stratovolcano in the Zambales Mountains in Luzon in the Philippines.

extra.why_interesting: All four are famous Southeast Asian volcanoes with similarly exotic names, so the player must actually know where the 1991 eruption happened to find the one outside Indonesia.
extra.verification_notes: Pinatubo is in the Philippines (Luzon), while Tambora, Merapi and Krakatoa are all in Indonesia.

explanation: Pinatubo is in the Philippines, and its huge 1991 eruption cooled the whole planet by about half a degree for a couple of years.

question: True or false: the Empire State Building in New York is struck by lightning more than ten times in a typical year.
source_excerpt: the skyscraper is struck by lightning 23 times a year

extra.why_interesting: The saying 'lightning never strikes twice' primes players to say false; the truth is that a tall tower gets hit over and over, every single year.
extra.verification_notes: Weather.com reports the Empire State Building is struck about 23 times a year (other sources say ~25), well above ten.

explanation: It takes around 20 to 25 strikes a year, which is exactly why scientists have long used it to study lightning and why the old saying is simply wrong.

question: Roughly how hot does the air inside a lightning bolt get, in degrees Celsius?
source_excerpt: air is heated to temperatures of 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit (about 30,000 °C)

extra.why_interesting: Players know lightning is hot but anchor on the Sun as the ultimate reference; discovering a bolt is several times hotter than the Sun's surface is the shock.
extra.verification_notes: NOAA states lightning heats the surrounding air to about 30,000 °C (54,000 °F), which is tens of thousands of degrees.

explanation: A bolt heats the air to around 30,000 degrees, about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun, and that violent expansion of air is what we hear as thunder.
